story: When a star wanders too close to a supermassive black hole, gravity rips it apart in a violent process called a tidal disruption event. First theorized in 1975 by Jack G. Hills, these cosmic cataclysms stretch stars into thin streams of glowing stellar debris. While about half of this shredded material escapes or forms a luminous accretion disk, roughly one percent launch powerful relativistic jets that beam bright radiation across the universe for years. Scientists first began observing these brilliant flares in the early 1990s using X-ray surveys, and today roughly one hundred events are known, helping astronomers uncover dormant black holes hiding quietly in the centers of normal galaxies.
